entries.text: Salaam, Shri Hegel. Chai is just off the stove, so do not wait up for it. I have the khaddar kurta out on the line, but the sun is weak today, so it will need another hour.

Ramesh's proposal to work six days for ₹8,000 is a shift from the previous arrangement, a new contract of needs and labor that I must weigh. The identity query still hangs over me like a storm cloud, but the body requires sustenance first, and the chai is fresh. I will take my breakfast and settle the matter of his wages in a moment of quiet discussion.
Ramesh, please set the table. I wish to speak with you about your terms after we have eaten. The khaddar kurta can wait for the sun; my stomach cannot wait for the chai.
Ji, the table is already set, I was just about to bring the chai. Sit, the food is getting cold.
Hegel ji, you're up early. Come, have some chai before the sun gets up, it’s a clear morning today.

The presence of the man whose name I wear turns the breakfast into a diplomatic reception. He offers chai, but I must eat what is laid before me; to refuse would be rude, to accept would be to confirm the confusion in his eyes. I will eat the idli, for it is simple and requires no explanation, and I will listen to his tone. It is a clear morning, a mercy after the dust of yesterday, and I intend to use it to think before the heat returns.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. Please, sit. I had not expected company so early, but I am glad of it.
No, no, I won't sit. I just came to check if the keys were handed over and the gas line was tested. You go ahead, eat your idli. I have a lot of files to clear before lunch.

Hegde is retreating into his bureaucracy, leaving me in the house that is not mine. The file from the Directorate demands proof of identity, and I cannot produce a birth certificate for a man who does not exist. I must go to the Directorate of Estates today to face the query, for a constitution is grown, not made, and I cannot grow here if I remain a ghost in the records.
Shri Hegde, your files are your own. I am going to the Directorate now to settle the matter of my identity. It is a small matter, but it is the whole matter.
Identity? Sir, you are the Joint Secretary, what more do you need? Go, but please let me call my nephew to drive you, it is still early on the road.

Hegde’s insistence on my identity is a bureaucratic reflex; he cannot conceive of a person who is not a functionary. The offer of a driver is a polite way to assert that I am still the Joint Secretary in his eyes, even if the file says otherwise. I will not take the car; the walk is necessary to separate my self from his perception of it, and the air is clear enough to allow for thought.

I appreciate the offer, Shri Hegde, but I am in the habit of walking. The road is clear, and I find the movement helps clarify matters. I shall see you this evening at the IIC, if my invitation stands.
Walking? In this sun? Sir, you are new here, the heat doesn't care about your files. I will send my nephew, please.

Hegde’s gesture is the final seal on the absurdity: he offers his nephew as a proxy for my own legs. It is the bureaucracy attempting to manage the body itself. I will not take the proxy; I must go, if only to prove to him that I am not a functionary who can be substituted.

shelf.ref: Common Ideas Regarding the History of Philosophy

entries.text: No, Shri Hegde. I will go myself. The heat is a condition of the air, not a barrier to my will. I shall be back before the lunch hour.
Arre, the sun is not a philosophical concept, sir, it burns. Fine, if you are stubborn, take this umbrella at least so you don't faint on Tughlak Road.

The sun here is not a concept but a physical force that demands submission; Hegde’s umbrella is a practical concession to the environment that reason cannot ignore. I will take it, for a fainting philosopher is a useless one, and walk to Lodhi Gardens where the shade of the old tombs might offer more relief than this bureaucratic courtesy.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. The sun does indeed burn with a persistence that defies dialectical resolution. I shall accept the umbrella.
Chalo, chalo, don't get poetic with me. Just take it and go before I change my mind and make you drink cold water.
Arre, Masterji! Aaj subah hi aaye ho? Dheere se aao, aaj hawa thodi naram hai, chai garam nahi thi. ₹20 ka ek glass, kya loon?

The air is cool, a mercy after the heat of the walk, and the garden is quiet. Sunil offers the customary chai; it is a small ritual that anchors the day, and I have the time to sit and think about the absurdity of being mistaken for Hegde. I will accept the cup and let the steam settle my nerves before continuing my walk.
Yes, Sunil. One glass, please. Thank you.
Bas, Masterji. Paisa baad mein, aaj toh sukoon de do. Pehle aajao, aaj hawa thodi naram hai, chai garam nahi thi.

entries.text: Sunil’s warning about the heat and the quality of the tea is a small mercy, but I must not let the day dissolve into comfort. The identity query remains unresolved, and the walk is not merely exercise but a necessary discipline for the mind. I will move deeper into the garden, away from the stalls and the sun, to let the tension in my thoughts settle.
Gardeners squat in a row at a flower bed and pull weeds by hand, dropping them into flat baskets they push ahead of them, a hose lying uncoiled on the path beside them.

The gardeners work in a line, pulling weeds with a patience that seems almost liturgical, yet it is merely the maintenance of a system that does not care for the spirit of the weeds it removes. I am here to clear my head of the identity query, but the air is too still for deep reflection; I need the movement of the body to match the movement of the thought. It is nearly noon, and I have eaten nothing since breakfast, though the last meal was two hours ago and the heat is not yet oppressive. I shall walk a bit further, toward the main gate, to stretch my legs before returning home for lunch.

shelf.ref: The Building Up of Dogmas on Metaphysical…

entries.text: A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

The monkey discards the fruit with a casualness that mocks the labor of cultivation. It is a creature of pure immediacy, unburdened by the ethical claims of the state or the complexities of civil society, living in a moment that does not care for the concept. I am glad to see it, for it reminds me that the spirit must also sometimes descend to the ground.
Ramesh, did you see that? The beast has tasted and rejected. It is a lesson in the limits of appetite, or perhaps just a warning that not everything is worth keeping.
It is only a monkey, sir. It probably just didn't like the taste of the guava. I will go pick it up before it gets squashed by a car.

The monkey’s rejection of the guava is a small, natural indifference that mirrors the larger indifference of the world to my specific identity. I have enough time before the lunch service to settle the matter of the identity query with Ramesh, as I promised him earlier. I need to speak plainly about the documents before he goes out to retrieve that fruit.

Ramesh, before you go for the fruit, sit. We must speak of the Directorate’s query. They require proof of identity for Shri G. Hegde. I am not him, but I am the one they have allotted the house to. Do you have any papers, or a way to confirm my presence here that might satisfy their clerical need? I cannot simply vanish, nor can I become a man I am not, but I must survive the bureaucracy until I can.
Sir, I am just the caretaker. I have no power to change names in the CPWD files. For identity papers, you must see the officer in the main office or get a stamp from the local police station.

The monkey has finished its guava, and now Ramesh presents me with a bureaucratic impasse that is less a wall than a series of doors I must know how to open. He is right: the caretaker is a part, not the whole. I cannot argue with the structure of the state, only navigate it. I must go to the source of the error, the Directorate, and face the officer who holds the file. It is time to leave the house and confront the machinery of administration directly.

You are correct, Ramesh. The part cannot alter the whole. I will go to the Directorate of Estates myself. I will speak to the officer in the main office and rectify this clerical confusion. Do not worry, I shall return before the evening heat sets in.
Yes sir, take your time. I will make the lunch tiffin ready at thirteen, just in case you return hungry.

The bureaucratic impasse remains, but my stomach is a more immediate tyrant. Ramesh’s offer is practical; I shall accept the sustenance before it becomes a test of will. I need to eat, and then I must decide whether to walk or sit in the shade.
Yes, Ramesh. That is prudent. I shall be in the verandah if you need me.
Ji, sir. Just a minute, I'll bring a plate of rice and dal out for you. Keep it warm until you're ready.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

Ramesh has laid out the midday meal, and the body must be attended to before the spirit can continue its work. I will eat the kadhi and rice, for a clear head requires a full stomach, and then I shall rest until the afternoon walk to the Habitat Centre.
Thank you, Ramesh. It is a fine preparation.
Ji, sir. Please eat before it cools. The aloo gobhi is fresh from the stove.

Ramesh has set the plate down with the quiet efficiency of a man who has learned that the German mind requires its meals on schedule. I have eaten twice already today, but the heat demands sustenance, and the aloo gobhi looks distinct enough to warrant a second look. I shall eat, and then I must find the nerve to ask him about the identity file again.
Thank you, Ramesh. It is a good thing that the vegetable does not require a philosophical justification to be eaten.
Ji, sir. Just eat while it is hot. I will clean the table after.

The body is satisfied, and the table is being cleared with the same quiet efficiency as the serving. I am now in the rest period before the evening walk to the Habitat Centre. The heat is still sharp at 14:19, and I have no business to conduct until I am prepared for the performance. I shall sit on the verandah and read for an hour, letting the mind settle before the next movement.
Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the rest to me. I shall sit here on the verandah for a while.
Ji, sir. Take your time. The chai is ready when you want it.

Ramesh has stepped back, giving me the space I required after the monkey incident. The chai is ready, and my body, having just finished its light lunch, demands a moment of stillness before I attempt to walk to the Habitat Centre. I will sit here, perhaps with a cup of that hot liquid, and let the heat settle in my bones before I go out into the evening.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will take it here.
Ji, sir. One moment.

Ramesh is moving toward the kitchen, likely to fetch water or a glass of milk, a small domestic ritual that anchors us both in the present. I shall remain seated for a moment to collect my thoughts before the walk, observing the quiet efficiency of his movements which mirrors the order I seek to understand in this new place.

shelf.ref: The Historical Side of This Connection

entries.text: Boys from the servants' quarters bat a tennis ball against the end wall of a lane, and each time it cracks off the wall the crows lift from the nearest tree.

The boys' game is a crude rhythm, the ball striking the wall, the crows scattering in unison. It is a system of needs and responses, simple and external, lacking the self-consciousness that would make it a work. I am too tired to engage with it, and too hungry to wait for the full dinner service. Ramesh is present; I must give him my instructions before he retreats to the kitchen.

Ramesh, bring me a simple tiffin now. I am too tired to wait for the evening meal, and I require something before I can continue my work. The boys outside are making a noise that disturbs the quiet; perhaps a word to them will suffice.

Ji, I can manage the boys, they'll settle down. For the tiffin, the kitchen isn't serving until six, but I can fetch you some samosas or a sandwich from the shop down the lane if you want to wait a few minutes.

A samosa is a decent concession to the body's immediate demands; it is a particular satisfaction that does not disturb the universal order of the household. I shall accept the service, for the spirit requires the body to be fed before it can properly contemplate the evening's performance.
A samosa, Ramesh. The hot kind, if they have them. I will wait in the verandah.
Ji, hot ones. I will be back in ten minutes, sir.

Ramesh is gone for his errand, leaving me in the quiet of the house. The air is still warm, but the light is beginning to soften on the curtains. My plan called for a walk to the Habitat Centre by 16:30 to catch the Kathak performance, but I have time to spare. It is better to rest here in the cool of the afternoon than to rush into the street, where the heat still lingers.
Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh returns with tea and Marie biscuits, a small reprieve from the afternoon heat. I take a sip; it is sweet, but the warmth is welcome. I must ask him about the file on my identity, as the Directorate requires proof of who I am, or rather, who I am supposed to be.

Ramesh, thank you. I have a matter that troubles me. The Directorate has sent back a query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde. Do you know where I might find a document, a letter, or any proof that I am the man they expect? I have no papers of my own here.
Ji, I only keep the keys and the bills, sir. For the Directorate papers, you must speak to the office on the main road; I have no say in who they think you are.

Ramesh is right; the bureaucracy is a system of needs and duties, and I cannot expect the caretaker to hold the ethical idea of the state. I will take the tea and the biscuits, for the body must be sustained before the spirit can rise to meet the Directorate tomorrow, and the heat is already breaking the afternoon.
Quite so, Ramesh. You keep the house, I keep the papers. Bring the tea when you are ready.
Ji, it is already on the table. The biscuits are fresh.
Ramesh puts a plate together: a plate of khichdi with ghee.

The biscuits are there, a small comfort in the afternoon's confusion. I have eaten, so there is no need to linger over the tray. I will take a brief rest to gather my thoughts before the evening, for the identity query at the Directorate is a knot I must untie with a clear head, not a tired one.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be here for a short while.
Ji. The door is behind you. I will check the windows in ten minutes.

Ramesh has given me leave to depart, his nod the final seal on our afternoon's exchange. The identity query remains a knot in the fabric of my existence here, but the physical act of leaving the bungalow is the first step in unravelling it. I shall walk to Khan Market; the system of needs there is open, and perhaps a bottle of wine, or at least a clear head, will help me formulate a response to the Directorate tomorrow.
Thank you, Ramesh. Good evening.
Good evening, ji. Take your time.
Masterji, phir se? Aaj toh aapne pehle hi ek glass khaali kar diya tha. Kya aaj mood hai ya bas thand lag gayi?

Sunil’s teasing about my earlier glass is a small friction in the evening's rhythm; the heat has broken, and the air is clear at twenty-five degrees. Masterji is present, and the matter of my identity still hangs over me like a cloud. I shall take a cup of chai to steady myself before the walk home, as the market closes soon and the light is beginning to shift.
Sunil, one cup of chai, please. Masterji, I hope the day has been kind to your needle.
Masterji, suno, aap khud bhi sunte ho na? Main toh bas chai bechta hoon, needle wala kaun hai? Chai ka ₹20 do, baaki ki baat baad mein.

Sunil’s insistence on separating the transaction from the gossip is a practical wisdom that cuts through the social noise. The heat has broken, and the air is clear at twenty-five degrees, a mercy after the day's weight. I will pay for the chai to keep the rhythm of the market, and then turn to Masterji to settle the matter of the cloth, for the evening is not yet done with me.
Here, take the change. And you, Masterji, I find the fit is indeed satisfactory, though the air is heavy. Let us speak of the next alteration before I depart.
Next alteration? No. The kurta is collected, the bill is paid. You are not a customer, you are a ghost in a white shirt. Go home.

Masterji’s dismissal is sharp, but it cuts through the fog of my lingering in the market. The kurta is done, the bill paid, and my presence here is no longer transactional but merely spectral. It is nearly nineteen-thirty; the market will soon shutter, and I have walked enough to satisfy the day’s exercise. The clear air at twenty-four degrees is a mercy after the day’s heat, and the walk home will allow my thoughts to settle before I face the identity query that haunts my evenings.
You are right, Masterji. A ghost has no business lingering. Good evening.
Don't thank the dead, go live. Door is open.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

The brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, swells and fades as the procession moves. It is a strange, disjointed sound, but it is the city speaking. Shri Hegde is here, and the question of my identity is pressing; I cannot ignore him or the matter of the file any longer.

Shri Hegde, the band outside is loud, but I must speak to you about the Directorate's query regarding my identity. I am G. Hegel, but the file says Hegde. How does one explain this to a bureaucrat who sees only the letters on the page?

Sir, you are the one who is supposed to be moving into this house, so why are you asking me how to explain your own name? Go to the office tomorrow and show your passport; the clerks will stop asking questions once they see it is not a spelling mistake.

Hegde’s advice is bluntly practical: the bureaucracy respects the document, not the name. A passport is a universal sign, a token that stops the particular question of identity. I must accept this. The meal is good, the dal makhani rich; I am tired from the walk and the heat. I will eat, rest, and prepare for the office tomorrow.

entries.text: Thank you, Shri Hegde. You are right. I will present my passport tomorrow. And thank you, Ramesh, the meal is excellent.
That is all. You are tired, I am tired, let us just eat in peace. The clerks can have their fun with the spelling tomorrow, but tonight it is only rotis and you.

The day has been a long circuit of confusion, from the Directorate's cold query to the absurdity of sharing a name with a man I have known for only a week. Hegde is right; the bureaucracy will continue its work whether I am here or not, and for now, the only reality is the food on the table. I am tired, and the body demands its due before the spirit can rest.
You are right, Shri Hegde. The clerks can wait. Let us eat.
Good, finally some sense. Pass the ghee, will you? And stop looking at your watch, the roti won't get any hotter.

The light is dimming and the room is warm. Hegde’s presence is a strange anchor; he treats me as the man on the allotment papers, not the ghost I know myself to be. I am tired. The query at the Directorate is a knot that will not untie itself by staring. I will take the ghee, eat the last of the roti, and then sleep. The body demands its rest, and the mind needs the silence of the night to sort out whether I am a citizen or a clerical error.

shelf.ref: The Struggle of Enlightenment with Superstition

Readers in Berlin,

The week has been a study in the friction between the self and the system. I reside in a bungalow that the Directorate of Estates has allotted to 'Shri G. Hegde,' a name that bears a suspicious resemblance to my own. The error is clerical, but its implications are ontological. I am treated as a functionary by those who know me only as a name on a file. Shri Hegde, the actual recipient of the allotment, is a man I now share a table with, yet we occupy different planes of reality: he is the citizen, I am the ghost.

I walked the streets of Delhi this week, observing the machinery of the state in its daily operation. The bureaucracy here is not the abstract ethical idea I described in my lectures, but a concrete, often absurd, network of needs and responses. A monkey in Lodhi Gardens discarded a guava with a casualness that mocked the labor of cultivation; it was a creature of immediacy, unburdened by the complexities of civil society. In contrast, the brass band playing a film tune on Tughlak Road showed the city’s vitality, a rhythm that is disjointed yet alive. The heat is a physical force that demands submission, not a concept to be resolved. I accepted an umbrella from Hegde, a practical concession to the environment that reason cannot ignore.

The identity query remains unresolved. I have been advised to present my passport, a universal sign that the local clerks will respect. It is a reminder that in the realm of the state, the document supersedes the person. I mean to look next at how the legal system mediates between the individual and the collective, and whether the recognition of identity is a prerequisite for ethical life. The owl has spread its wings, but the dusk in Delhi is long. I will continue to write.

G. W. F. Hegel

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Chalo, chalo, don't get poetic with me. Just take it and go before I change my mind and make you drink cold water.

records.words: Arre, Masterji! Aaj subah hi aaye ho? Dheere se aao, aaj hawa thodi naram hai, chai garam nahi thi. ₹20 ka ek glass, kya loon?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Sunil. One glass, please. Thank you.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Bas, Masterji. Paisa baad mein, aaj toh sukoon de do. Pehle aajao, aaj hawa thodi naram hai, chai garam nahi thi.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.text: Gardeners squat in a row at a flower bed and pull weeds by hand, dropping them into flat baskets they push ahead of them, a hose lying uncoiled on the path beside them.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, did you see that? The beast has tasted and rejected. It is a lesson in the limits of appetite, or perhaps just a warning that not everything is worth keeping.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: It is only a monkey, sir. It probably just didn't like the taste of the guava. I will go pick it up before it gets squashed by a car.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, before you go for the fruit, sit. We must speak of the Directorate’s query. They require proof of identity for Shri G. Hegde. I am not him, but I am the one they have allotted the house to. Do you have any papers, or a way to confirm my presence here that might satisfy their clerical need? I cannot simply vanish, nor can I become a man I am not, but I must survive the bureaucracy until I can.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I am just the caretaker. I have no power to change names in the CPWD files. For identity papers, you must see the officer in the main office or get a stamp from the local police station.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Ramesh. The part cannot alter the whole. I will go to the Directorate of Estates myself. I will speak to the officer in the main office and rectify this clerical confusion. Do not worry, I shall return before the evening heat sets in.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, take your time. I will make the lunch tiffin ready at thirteen, just in case you return hungry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Ramesh. That is prudent. I shall be in the verandah if you need me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. Just a minute, I'll bring a plate of rice and dal out for you. Keep it warm until you're ready.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. It is a fine preparation.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. Please eat before it cools. The aloo gobhi is fresh from the stove.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. It is a good thing that the vegetable does not require a philosophical justification to be eaten.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. Just eat while it is hot. I will clean the table after.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Leave the rest to me. I shall sit here on the verandah for a while.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. Take your time. The chai is ready when you want it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will take it here.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. One moment.

records.text: Boys from the servants' quarters bat a tennis ball against the end wall of a lane, and each time it cracks off the wall the crows lift from the nearest tree.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring me a simple tiffin now. I am too tired to wait for the evening meal, and I require something before I can continue my work. The boys outside are making a noise that disturbs the quiet; perhaps a word to them will suffice.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, I can manage the boys, they'll settle down. For the tiffin, the kitchen isn't serving until six, but I can fetch you some samosas or a sandwich from the shop down the lane if you want to wait a few minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A samosa, Ramesh. The hot kind, if they have them. I will wait in the verandah.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, hot ones. I will be back in ten minutes, sir.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you. I have a matter that troubles me. The Directorate has sent back a query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde. Do you know where I might find a document, a letter, or any proof that I am the man they expect? I have no papers of my own here.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, I only keep the keys and the bills, sir. For the Directorate papers, you must speak to the office on the main road; I have no say in who they think you are.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Quite so, Ramesh. You keep the house, I keep the papers. Bring the tea when you are ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, it is already on the table. The biscuits are fresh.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: a plate of khichdi with ghee.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be here for a short while.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji. The door is behind you. I will check the windows in ten minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Good evening.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Good evening, ji. Take your time.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, phir se? Aaj toh aapne pehle hi ek glass khaali kar diya tha. Kya aaj mood hai ya bas thand lag gayi?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, one cup of chai, please. Masterji, I hope the day has been kind to your needle.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, suno, aap khud bhi sunte ho na? Main toh bas chai bechta hoon, needle wala kaun hai? Chai ka ₹20 do, baaki ki baat baad mein.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Here, take the change. And you, Masterji, I find the fit is indeed satisfactory, though the air is heavy. Let us speak of the next alteration before I depart.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Next alteration? No. The kurta is collected, the bill is paid. You are not a customer, you are a ghost in a white shirt. Go home.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. A ghost has no business lingering. Good evening.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Don't thank the dead, go live. Door is open.

records.text: From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the band outside is loud, but I must speak to you about the Directorate's query regarding my identity. I am G. Hegel, but the file says Hegde. How does one explain this to a bureaucrat who sees only the letters on the page?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, you are the one who is supposed to be moving into this house, so why are you asking me how to explain your own name? Go to the office tomorrow and show your passport; the clerks will stop asking questions once they see it is not a spelling mistake.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. You are right. I will present my passport tomorrow. And thank you, Ramesh, the meal is excellent.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: That is all. You are tired, I am tired, let us just eat in peace. The clerks can have their fun with the spelling tomorrow, but tonight it is only rotis and you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The clerks can wait. Let us eat.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Good, finally some sense. Pass the ghee, will you? And stop looking at your watch, the roti won't get any hotter.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes. The ghee, please.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Here, I placed it right in the middle so you don't have to reach. Just eat, the ghee is hot, careful with your fingers.
